rationale: The hypothesis posits that systemic lactate elevations in MMDS9B are mild and intermittent and that MRS brain lactate peaks occur in no more than 30% of patients. However, the available literature directly dealing with FDXR-associated disease presents contradictory findings. While general iron-sulfur cluster assembly defects (such as FDX2) show MRS lactate peaks in roughly 25% of evaluated patients (e.g., 1 of 4 in Gurgel 2018), cohorts and neuroimaging reviews specifically evaluating FDXR mitochondriopathy document that blood lactate is frequently increased and cerebral MRS classically demonstrates a markedly elevated lactate peak, particularly during acute decompensations or in the basal ganglia and brainstem. Other reports note variable or absent lactate outside of acute episodes, confirming that lactate elevation is inconsistent, but the specific numerical threshold (<=30%) is contradicted by cohorts where lactate peaks were readily detected.

evidence.text: In FDXR-related mitochondriopathy, MR spectroscopy will classically reveal a markedly elevated lactate peak affecting the basal ganglia or brainstem during acute or equivocal presentations, rather than merely mild elevations.

conflicts: Lam et al. (2026) report that MRS will 'classically reveal a markedly elevated lactate peak' in decompensated/equivocal FDXR cases, contrasting with the hypothesis that elevations are consistently mild.

Vanlander and Van Coster (2018) describe elevated blood lactate and cerebral lactate peaks in FDXR cohorts, conflicting with the claim that brain lactate peaks are limited to <=30% of assessed patients.

The 25% to 30% MRS lactate peak prevalence appears generalized from broader iron-sulfur cluster deficiencies (such as FDX2, where 1 of 4 individuals had an MRS lactate peak) rather than consistently verified in FDXR/MMDS9B cohorts.
